blocks.html: To execute is nothing other than to effect, accomplish and finish something; whence executors, in our laws, are properly called those who bring to an end and effect the judgment of the judge a2. And by the same reason, in the matter of last wills, Executors are called those who have the charge of effecting and accomplishing the will of the deceased b; of whom the interpreters have been accustomed to make three kinds, namely Testamentary, Legitimate and Dative [Donnez, "given"]. Testamentary are those to whom the deceased, in his testament, has given the charge of effecting his will c, be they laymen or clerks, secular or regular; for even religious, with leave (however) of their superior, may be executors of testaments d, the Cordeliers alone excepted e — as to whom, moreover, some teach that a Guardian of Saint Francis, although he cannot be executor of a testament f, if nevertheless he has been left executor and has executed, no one opposing or gainsaying, the execution is valid g; inasmuch as this charge is not forbidden to the religious of this order for the defect or vice of their persons, but for the estate and perfection (as one says) of their rule h. And therefore, in like terms, priests and clerks in holy orders, to whom it is not permitted to exercise the office of tabellion or notary, if nevertheless they receive instruments, the parties not gainsaying, such instruments are good and valid i. Now these testamentary executors, because they are bound to render account and pay over the balance remaining k, must (after the example of guardians l), before all else, make an inventory of the goods of the deceased m, without which one could not afterwards recover from them accounts or the payment of the balance n. Legitimate executors are those to whom this charge and faculty is given by the law, as is the Bishop o, who must watch over and provide that the pious wills of the deceased be both faithfully and entirely accomplished p. And to these ends he must admonish, twice at the least, the heir or the testamentary executor (if there is any) to pay, or cause to be paid, the bequests made to the poor or to other pious works; and he who does not satisfy this on his part within the year shall lose all the profit which he could otherwise gather from the testamentary disposition r. Which the bishop may do although the deceased had expressly forbidden the bishop to meddle in it ſ, inasmuch as such prohibitions are private [unclear: priuées; perhaps for praves, "perverse"] and little reasonable, nay, seem to contain ineptitude and some impiety t; wherefore they cannot hinder the force of equitable laws, the virtue of the holy constitutions u. And if the bishop were negligent in making the aforesaid admonitions and procuring the accomplishment of such wills, recourse must be had to the Metropolitan x. Dative executors are those whom the Judge, consul or other magistrate appoints, the heirs of the deceased having been called.
